world.setting: Cases across time - Darwin's London study (1838), Franklin's letter (1772), Collect Pond in 1802 Manhattan, the CIA and White House rooms of 2010-2011, Meadow Lake in Queens, George Eliot's Victorian desk - set against a modern listener's kitchen table, office and conference room.

everyman.name: The Listener
everyman.role: the contemporary listener facing a big choice: a job offer, a house, a hire, a launch, a partnership
everyman.look: A 34-year-old American professional with short dark brown hair, wearing a teal casual button-up shirt and grey chinos.

darwin.name: Charles Darwin
darwin.role: naturalist who weighs marriage on a two-column list in 1838, and later weighs publishing his theory against his wife's faith
darwin.look: A Victorian English gentleman of about 30 with a receding hairline, brown muttonchop sideburns, a black frock coat and white high collar.

emma.name: Emma Darwin
emma.role: Darwin's wife, whose faith after their daughter's death his theory would wound
emma.look: A Victorian Englishwoman in her thirties with dark hair parted in the middle in a low bun, wearing a deep plum high-necked dress.

franklin.name: Benjamin Franklin
franklin.role: invents 'moral algebra' in a 1772 letter to Priestley
franklin.look: An elderly 18th-century American statesman, balding with long grey hair at the sides, small round spectacles, brown wool coat.

priestley.name: Joseph Priestley
priestley.role: scientist agonizing over a job offer from the Earl of Shelburne; Franklin's friend
priestley.look: An 18th-century English clergyman-scientist of about 40 with short brown hair, a plain black coat and a white clerical neckband.

lenfant.name: Pierre L'Enfant
lenfant.role: French architect who proposes cleaning Collect Pond and making it a public park
lenfant.look: A French architect of about 50 in 1802, dark hair tied back, navy blue tailcoat with a rolled plan under his arm.

alderman.name: The City Council
alderman.role: the 1802 New York council and developers who reduce Collect Pond to a binary and fill it in
alderman.look: A stout New York merchant-alderman of 1802 with grey sideburns, black top hat and a mustard waistcoat under a dark coat.

brennan.name: John Brennan
brennan.role: counterterrorism adviser who demands the analysts disprove their own theory
brennan.look: A balding American official in his fifties with short grey hair at the sides, a charcoal suit, white shirt and dark red tie.

analyst.name: The CIA Analyst
analyst.role: intelligence analyst mapping the Abbottabad compound and building the case
analyst.look: A 38-year-old woman analyst with a dark brown ponytail, glasses, a light blue blouse under a navy cardigan and an ID badge.

ceo.name: The CEO
ceo.role: the boss at the head of the table whom everyone agrees with too quickly
ceo.look: A confident man of 55 with slicked silver hair in a navy three-piece suit and light blue tie.

colleague.name: The Dissenting Colleague
colleague.role: the cognitively peripheral voice in the room: holds the unshared fact, a juror from a different background
colleague.look: A 30-year-old Black woman with natural curly hair, wearing a mustard yellow blazer over a black top.

johnson.name: Steven Johnson
johnson.role: the author, weighing a move from Brooklyn to Marin County with his wife
johnson.look: An American writer around 45 with short sandy-brown hair, light stubble and glasses, wearing a green flannel shirt.

wife.name: Johnson's Wife
wife.role: weighs her Brooklyn friendships against California
wife.look: A woman around 45 with shoulder-length auburn hair, wearing a burgundy sweater and dark jeans.

eliot.name: George Eliot
eliot.role: Victorian novelist writing Middlemarch at her desk
eliot.look: A Victorian Englishwoman of about 50 with brown hair parted in the centre over the ears, wearing a dark grey dress with a white lace collar.

dorothea.name: Dorothea Brooke
dorothea.role: Middlemarch's idealistic heroine choosing whether to marry Casaubon
dorothea.look: A young Victorian woman of 19 with dark chestnut hair in braids, wearing a plain pale lavender dress.

casaubon.name: Mr. Casaubon
casaubon.role: the dry, pedantic old scholar Dorothea is drawn to marry
casaubon.look: A gaunt Victorian scholar of about 50 with thin white hair, a black scholar's coat and a book always in hand.

room.look: A Victorian study with a wooden desk, ink and a notebook under a sooty window (Darwin, Franklin, Priestley).

office.look: A secure modern meeting room: a long table, a scale model in the middle, screens on the wall (CIA, White House, corporate meetings).

kitchen.look: A quiet modern kitchen at midnight with a yellow legal pad on the table.

shore.look: The edge of a pond or lake: Collect Pond in 1802 Manhattan, Meadow Lake in Queens choked with algae.

street.look: A city street: old lower Manhattan, the Five Points slum, a Brooklyn block.

court.look: A jury room or courtroom where mock juries deliberate.

library.look: A book-lined study for George Eliot writing Middlemarch and Casaubon's scholarship.

horizon.look: An open landscape for futures, California hills and the long view.

sky.look: A night sky for messages to the stars and people not yet born.

abstract.look: A clean canvas for maps, lists, diagrams and options A, B and C.

objects.why: Darwin's Marry / Not Marry page, Franklin's moral algebra, the midnight legal pad - the two-column list the book calls an evaluation tool, not a discovery tool.
The recurring 'widen the map before you choose': two obvious roads and the invented third path (L'Enfant's park, the counter-offer, the two-year experiment).
The table-sized scale model of the Abbottabad compound the CIA studied for months.
The luxury houses built on filled-in Collect Pond that sank, flooded and became Five Points.
The dog in the compound - the contrary evidence the red team found.
The Black Hawk raid option whose lift in heat and altitude had to be modelled.
Tetlock's hedgehog: one big theory, one predicted future.
Tetlock's fox: many small ideas, multiple futures.
Weighing values: Franklin's cancelling, linear value modelling.
The premortem - the plan imagined already dead.
Messages to the stars; the far future.

signatureObjects.name: The two-column pros and cons list
signatureObjects.why: Darwin's and Franklin's list is the book's foil; the shared 'notes' icon is a generic page and loses the two columns.

signatureObjects.name: Option C - the third path
signatureObjects.why: The book's core mechanism (widen the map): no shared icon shows two roads plus an invented third.

signatureObjects.name: The Abbottabad compound model
signatureObjects.why: The CIA's scale model is the book's image of mapping; no shared icon depicts it.

signatureObjects.name: The sinking houses of Collect Pond
signatureObjects.why: The consequence of filling the pond: houses sinking into marsh, the birth of Five Points.

signatureObjects.name: The dog in the compound
signatureObjects.why: The red-team detail that nearly broke the theory.

signatureObjects.name: The raid helicopters
signatureObjects.why: The scenario the planners modelled (lift, heat, altitude) and the premortem's crash.

signatureObjects.name: Tetlock's fox
signatureObjects.why: Many-small-ideas forecaster who models multiple futures.

spine.claim: Our worst decisions fail at the moment we accept only two options - Darwin's two-column list and the city that filled in Collect Pond instead of building L'Enfant's park.
A pros-and-cons list only evaluates; mapping hidden variables, a messy divergence phase and diverse rooms that surface hidden profiles discover the real terrain.
Predicting means telling several futures - Brennan's red team, scenario planning, foxes over hedgehogs, the 70% rule and the premortem that builds escape hatches.
Deciding means weighing values openly - Johnson's Brooklyn-or-California deadlock became an invented option C - and fiction like Middlemarch rehearses choices numbers cannot.
We rarely have nine months, so we train on the big choices until seeing wider is reflex: farsightedness is seeing wider, not further.
